paragraphs.text: Here St. Paul affirms that the apostolic ministry he performs was not entrusted to him by a man, but by God the Father, who accomplished salvation for us through His Son Jesus Christ, our hope that will not disappoint.

The Apostle addresses the Epistle to his disciple Timothy, whom he calls “my own son.” The Greek word translated here as “own” is “genesios,” which means genuine or true; so he regards Timothy as a true son to him, and likewise he bears witness to the genuineness of his faith and his labor in preaching the Gospel. As is usual in the epistles of Paul, he asks grace from God for all, and here he adds mercy as well, by which God lifted us out of a state of enmity into sonship. He asks for them the peace that Christ promised to give us, the peace that passes all understanding. And the Apostle here affirms the oneness of the source of grace, mercy and peace, and the oneness of work between the Father and the Son, when he says, “from God our Father and Jesus Christ our Lord.”

May you be confident of God who is with you and who commands you to be a light to the world, so that you hold fast to truth and love in all your dealings, even if all the others walk in evil. Do not be shaken, trusting in the power of God that upholds you.

After the Apostle was released from his first imprisonment in Rome in AD 63, he went to Macedonia and asked Timothy to remain in Ephesus in order to forbid the strange doctrines preached by some priests and teachers (Acts 20:30) and to bring them back to the right faith, because some preached Judaizing and others preached Gnosticism, as we mentioned in the introduction to the Epistle.
Fables: imaginary tales with which the myths of the Greeks and the Romans are filled.
Genealogies: the Jews’ pride in tracing the Levites to Aaron or the tribe of Judah to David, and likewise the concern of the Gentiles for their lineage back to great men.
Endless: without benefit and without purpose.

Questions: the disputes of the Gnostics, who believe that knowledge is salvation, and so argue proudly to establish their opinions. This is utterly far from faith, which is the way of salvation, and from which spiritual studies and inquiries spring.

The Apostle warns them to keep away from believing and being influenced by the talk of myths or from boasting in genealogies, because this breeds pride and draws them into harmful disputes that turn them away from building their spiritual life and growing in Christ.

Love is the goal of the commandment, and the Lord of glory affirmed this truth in His reply to the lawyer, as it is written in (Mt 22:35-39), that on the commandment of love hang all the Law and the Prophets. And for this love to be genuine, it must spring from a heart sanctified by God’s dwelling in it, from a good intention untouched by any malice, and from sincere faith.
If a person turns aside from sincere divine love and from faith, he turns away from the godly life and true witness to talk that profits nothing and to aimless questionings.

Examine your love toward others: is it for God’s sake, or according to your personal liking, or does it have material aims? May you care for everyone even if you have no interest in them, be gentle with offenders whom people shun, and pray for all.

entries.section: (3) The Law makes us aware of the need for salvation

paragraphs.text: These people of whom St. Paul speaks are of Jewish origin; they follow position and love of leadership, seek fame and demand honor, while in truth they are far from knowing the goal of the Law. They multiply discussions and disputes, not out of a desire to reach the truth, but in order to impose their authority on people.

entries.section: (3) The Law makes us aware of the need for salvation

paragraphs.text: Uses it lawfully: understands the spirit of the Law and applies it carefully for God’s sake.

So that no one misunderstands St. Paul and thinks that he is accusing the Law and condemning it, or condemning teaching as something not good, he affirms that the fault is not in the Law, for it is good and holy, but in its misuse.

entries.section: (3) The Law makes us aware of the need for salvation

paragraphs.text: The Law was made not for the righteous but for the wicked, because the righteous can grasp the commandments of the Law through their natural conscience, whereas for the wicked it is the Law that can keep them from sin by frightening them with punishment. Here the Apostle mentions kinds of wicked people: the lawless, who are sinners ... the disobedient, who are those who break the commandment deliberately ... the ungodly, who are those who commit sin without shame or modesty ... sinners, who are those who commit transgressions ... the unholy, who are those defiled by sins and iniquities ... the profane, who are those who sin without the least reproach from their consciences ... murderers of fathers and mothers, who represent the hardest kinds of hearts ... manslayers, who make light of the lives of others.

entries.section: (3) The Law makes us aware of the need for salvation

paragraphs.text: Whoremongers: those who defile their bodies.
Them that defile themselves with mankind: those who are sexually perverse.
Menstealers: those who seize the property of others without right. Liars: those who do not tell the truth in pursuit of material gain. Perjured persons: those who do not keep their promise.
Whatever is contrary to sound doctrine: those who resist the true teaching. For the sake of these and their like, God gave His Law, that they might feel the need for salvation.

entries.section: (3) The Law makes us aware of the need for salvation

paragraphs.text: Sound doctrine is the joyful good news that shows the greatness of the blessed God, and it is the teaching that St. Paul passed on faithfully, as the divine will willed to make him a faithful witness to the soundness of the teaching.
May you benefit from God’s commandments and apply them in your life, for every teaching you hear is a message to you. Do not hurry to rebuke and teach others while forgetting your own personal life.
St. Paul thanks God because He counted him faithful and strengthened him and called him to His service despite his unworthiness.
In humility St. Paul confesses his former sins before believing, which are:
1- Blaspheming Christ and describing Him as a mere ordinary man.
2- Persecuting the Christians by arresting them, torturing them and killing them.
3- Slandering them with false charges in order to put them on trial and torture them.

At the same time God’s great mercy appears in forgiving these sins, and even in turning him into a minister and preacher, because he did these evils from not knowing Christ; and when Christ appeared to him, he repented and turned back from his sins.
In addition to making him a minister, God’s grace overflowed upon him with many spiritual gifts and fruits, besides his first enjoying the Christian faith and love for God and love for every person.

St. Paul declares the truth of God’s word, which gladdens a person who receives it and enjoys it, and this word is that Christ became incarnate to save sinners, that is, all humanity; and in humility and repentance he declares himself the chief of sinners because of his persecution of the Christians mentioned before.

Paul shows God’s wisdom and love in accepting him despite his sins and turning him into a minister, for this shows God’s longsuffering toward sinners, so as to encourage all the wicked to return to God, not only that He may forgive them but that He may give them the Kingdom of Heaven.

The Apostle ends his discourse on God’s mercy by glorifying Him, declaring some of His attributes: that He is eternal, that He is King in every age, that He is too high for anyone to see, and that in Him is all wisdom and honor.
What happened with Paul encourages us all to repent, however great or repeated our sins may be, and it urges us to a positive life with God through good works and serving others.
This commandment: Christ is the Savior of sinners, so we rely on Him.

The prophecies: there were earlier prophecies about Timothy, that he would live with God and be His minister. War a good warfare: strive in relying on God and in encouraging all sinners to repent so that they may obtain eternal life.
If God chose Timothy and declared that in prophecies about him, then Paul charges him to care for the salvation of his own soul and to call sinners to repentance.
Faith: reliance on the power of Christ working in him.
A good conscience: purity and sincerity in loving God and serving Him.
Having put away: some, that is, the heretics.
Have made shipwreck concerning faith: they went astray and sank, that is, they departed from Christ, and their hope and faith were lost.
The Apostle calls him to hold fast to the faith and purity of heart which the heretics rejected, and so went on the way of perdition.
Hymenaeus: he is also mentioned in (2 Tim 2:17), where Paul describes him as having erred concerning the truth, saying that the resurrection is past already, and so overthrowing the faith of some.
Alexander: he is the one mentioned in (2 Tim 4:14), “Alexander the coppersmith did me much evil: the Lord reward him according to his works.”

The pride of their hearts led these two persons to invent unsound teachings; therefore St. Paul decided to judge them by cutting them off from the fellowship of the Church, so that they would not corrupt the thoughts of the believers, and at the same time, by being deprived of fellowship, they might return to God in repentance. For the Apostle does not seek vengeance by the punishment, but asks for discipline that leads to correction.
Commandments concerning worship

After showing God’s mercy to all sinners, St. Paul declares the first of his teachings to Timothy in his shepherding of the Church, which is that he should call the believers to feel for all people, so that they offer up to Him their prayers for the needs of all and likewise give thanks to God for His gifts to all people.

It is fitting for us to care for everyone as our heavenly Father does, for this is the message of the Church, whether at the communal or the individual level; we do not ask only for what is for ourselves, but also for what is for others. And as the Church practices these kinds of prayers in her liturgical prayers, as in the Divine Liturgy, may you too, in your prayer, take care to ask for others, especially those who asked you to pray for them and those who have no one to remember them, that is, the despised and the rejected.

The Church is not an institution that competes with the world for what belongs to it, but a community that worships God for the sanctification of the world. So she offers supplications, prayers and intercessions for kings and rulers and those in positions of leadership, that God’s peace may come upon the land and that this may help the believers grow in godliness and the fear of God.

And these prayers for others gladden God’s heart and make our prayers acceptable and good before Him. We find in the Liturgy of St. Basil, before the prayer of reconciliation, the litany for the peace of the Church, and in the Liturgy of St. Gregory a litany for the king or president or those who serve in the court (the palace), and for all who work in the state and the soldiers, for their peace.

God rejoices in our prayers for everyone because He desires the salvation of all and calls them to know Him, for He is the true God, and so He rescues them from the error of idols and the sins of the world.

Here the Apostle sets forth a truth of faith, which is that there is one Mediator between God and men, and He is the incarnate Christ. He set this forth to refute what the Gnostics claimed of successive emanations from God, which they called “aeons,” that bring knowledge to people as the way of salvation. In their view Christ is the first step, that is, the first aeon, who raises man by knowledge to a greater aeon, and so on, until he reaches perfect knowledge, the Supreme Being.

So the Apostle replies to this and says that Christ is the only Mediator of atonement, and not the many mediating gods proclaimed by the Gnostics. And this, of course, has no relation to the intercession of the saints before God, because some use this verse to oppose our belief in the intercession of the saints; but it has nothing to do with intercession, rather it is a reply to the Gnostics.

The testimony: Christ’s redemption of humanity and the offering of His blood as atonement and justification for everyone who believes in Him. In due time: the time appointed by God for the redemption of man, that is, the time in which Christ died and rose.
Christ gave His life on the Cross, and by this He testified before the Father to the possibility of justifying man, so that everyone who believes in Him may enter into eternal life.

This is the salvation that St. Paul preaches, proclaiming the true faith to the Gentiles who were formerly idolaters, as God’s grace extended to embrace all humanity and the knowledge of the truth was no longer confined to one nation to the exclusion of another.

Christ bore witness to your righteousness before God by His death on the Cross; so you too must bear witness by your purity and your love for everyone, that Christ may be glorified in your good works.
Every where: Jewish worship was only in the temple at Jerusalem, but the churches of the New Testament are everywhere, in addition to private prayers in the inner room.
Holy hands: he means purity of body and spirit, so that men do not allow themselves uncleanness, for their prayers would not be accepted.
Without wrath: men are quick to anger, so he warns them to control themselves and keep their inner peace so that they may be able to pray and to sense God.
Doubting: men tend to rely on reason, and this may cast them into a troublesome debate that robs them of their peace, so he warns them against this so that they may concentrate in their prayers.

The Apostle calls the believing men to pray in their churches and their homes, joining their prayers with pure conduct, keeping away from anger and pride and the useless debate that results from them.
Modest apparel: clothing that is not a stumbling block.
Godliness: piety and the fear of God, that is, their conduct is fitting for daughters of God.
Sobriety: composure and not being preoccupied with appearance.
Broided hair: some women used to make dozens of braids in their hair, which consumed much time and attention, so the Apostle forbids excessive concern for adornment.
Gold or pearls: he means being preoccupied with adorning oneself abundantly with jewels.
He calls the believing women to commit to modest clothing that is not a stumbling block, as women who fear God, and not to be absorbed in adornment, whether in hair or ornaments or clothes.
Here he adds the positive side, for she who professes to live to God will surely care about her good works, and not only about keeping away from causing others to stumble.

The Apostle asks the woman not to speak in the church, but to hear the words of preaching from the man and to submit to his leadership, for this suits her and gives her rest as a woman; and he certainly does not mean to despise her or belittle her, because she can surpass the man in her holiness according to her faith and her life with God.

The Apostle forbids women to teach men, because leadership and teaching suit the man, and the woman is a help meet for him who completes him and supports him. The nature of the man does not accept teaching and leadership from the woman, whereas it suits the woman to be led and taught by the man. But the woman’s abstaining from teaching the man does not hinder her from teaching women, girls and children.
The idea of the woman’s submission to the man is not born of human thought, but is a divine order realized in creation, for God created Adam first and after him created the woman as a helper for him.

The serpent deceived Eve, and she broke the commandment, but Adam was not deceived, though he fell under Eve’s influence, for she is more exposed to deception. In this verse St. Paul shows us why a woman ought not to take up teaching: because she is affected more quickly than the man by her emotions, and so she may deviate from sound teaching, and it does not suit her to lead the teaching. But she can be more spiritual than the man through her emotions if she uses them well.

Just as the man has the responsibility of leadership and teaching, which qualifies him to obtain the heavenly crowns, so the woman has her responsibilities, such as raising her sons and daughters in virtue and helping them grow spiritually, so that she presents to the Church blessed members; and by this she has a share in the crowns of glory, on condition that she continue in faith and love and holiness with wisdom, which is the true adornment of a woman.

Do not be distracted from the love of Christ by any earthly matter, and so you will be able to open yourself in prayer with a pure heart and enjoy the divine sense; and what helps you in this is to put the fear of God before your eyes, so that you reject every sin and keep your purity.
The Church and the requirements for the priestly ranks

The responsibilities of the bishop are great, because he bears the responsibility of leading the Church, and he is exposed to persecutions and troubles from outside and from within. So St. Paul declares that whoever loves God and desires to consecrate his life to Him in the service of the priesthood, this is a good thing that gladdens God’s heart. It is to be noted that he mentioned the qualifications of the bishop and then the qualifications of the deacon, because by “bishop” he means the priesthood in general, that is, the bishop and the priest.
St. Paul makes clear the qualities that must be found in him, which are:
Blameless: that is, without clear sins that cause others to stumble; he does not mean any sin in the heart, because there is no person without sin.
The husband of one wife: married once, or not married again after being widowed; this declares his chastity by being content with a single marriage.
Vigilant: alert, watchful, cautious, of keen insight, mindful of the salvation of his own soul and of those he shepherds. Sober: steady, acting with wisdom and moderation.
Of good behaviour: modest in his appearance, his conduct and his speech, keeping away from frivolity.

Given to hospitality: hosting strangers is a sign of a wide heart. In the early Christian period the believers moved about much because of persecution, and therefore the bishop’s house had to be open to them.
Apt to teach: he has the gift of teaching, founded on right spiritual knowledge.

Not given to wine: wine is not forbidden, but there is no need for it. What is forbidden is excessive drinking that leads to drunkenness, and this is of course a quality rejected in a bishop, and it means not being absorbed in general in the enjoyment of food and drink.

No striker: that is, one who strikes often and is quick to use it as a means of correcting those who are spiritually deviant. Not greedy of filthy lucre: not a lover of money, especially what he gets through improper conduct, such as giving up what is right to please some of the rich; rather, money is only a means for service and for supporting the needy, and he does not care whether he has it or not.
Patient: patient with his spiritual children, not flaring up at their mistakes but bringing them back to the truth with all patience.

Not a brawler: he does not break the bond of affection and relationship with any of his children, whatever the reasons. Not covetous: the love of money is the root of all evil, so it is not fitting that it should possess the heart of the bishop, who is supposed to be an example of goodness.
He leads and manages his house soundly and brings up his children well, so that they obey him and submit to the Christian teachings and principles that he teaches them.
Whoever cannot give heed to his children and care for them as he ought will not be able to do this in the wider circle, which is the church of God.
Not a novice: not one who has believed only a short while.
Lifted up with pride: that is, becoming arrogant.

The condemnation of the devil: he falls into many sins for which Satan accuses him before God. The Apostle warns against being hasty in ordaining a person who began to attach himself to the Church and to serve only a short time ago, because by this he is exposed to pride, thinking himself better than those who preceded him in the Church, and this creates many problems.
The bishop must have a good reputation, and his goodness must be clear and his former conduct above reproach, so that Satan does not use his enemies or unbelievers to condemn and blame him.
These qualifications apply to every servant and every spiritual person, so examine yourself on the basis of these qualities and strive to acquire the one you find you need most.
The deacons: what is meant here is the full deacon, that is, the diaconos, and not the preliminary ranks such as reader and chanter, in which most deacons are ordained at present.
As the Apostle specified in the previous verses the qualities that must be found in the bishop, here he specifies them for the candidates for the diaconate, which are:
That they be grave: that is, of refined, steady conduct.
Not doubletongued: that they not be deceitful.
Not given to much wine: this is the same quality required in the bishop and mentioned in (v. 3). Not greedy of filthy lucre: this too was mentioned before in (v. 3).

The mystery of the faith: Christ the Savior of the whole world, Jews and Gentiles, whatever their sins; it is called a mystery because the love of Christ the Savior surpasses intellectual comprehension.
The deacon must have strong faith with a pure conscience, that is, sincerity without personal aim.

Before deacons are ordained, they must first be proved by serving faithfully and lovingly, and their conduct in their former and present life is likewise proved. If the result of the proving is positive, which St. Paul expresses by the phrase “blameless,” they are then qualified for the rank of deacon.
The discourse here does not concern women in general, but concerns deaconesses or consecrated women or the wives of deacons, and the qualities required in them are as follows:
Grave: as mentioned in the qualities of deacons and priests.
Not slanderers: they do not speak of the faults of others.
Sober: mindful of their spiritual life.

Faithful in all things: sincere, for by their position they are privy to the secrets of homes, so they must be faithful with the secrets entrusted to them, faithful in distributing alms, faithful in the holy commandments.
As mentioned in (vv. 2, 4)
The Apostle shows the blessing of the service of the diaconate, which helps the one who holds it to grow in faith in Christ through his service.
The place, the work and the circumstances that God has given you, whether you are a servant in the Church or a father or a mother, be faithful in them and ask God’s help to glorify Him through them.

St. Paul promises Timothy to come to him, in order to reassure him and encourage him and affirm to him that, as he has guided and directed him by this epistle, he will support him by his personal presence with him in Ephesus.
Behave thyself: manage the Church and lead the ministry in it.
The pillar and ground of the truth: the support of the truth, for the Church, by the strong faith in Christ within her, proclaims and supports the truth in the whole world.

The Apostle affirms to his disciple Timothy that he will come to him, but if he is delayed in coming he should not be distressed, because this will be by the permission of the Holy Spirit, so that Timothy may have more opportunity to work and to exert more effort as a servant of the church of the living God, which the Apostle calls the house of God. And he defined the features of the Church as resting on the truth, which is the foundation of faith, and not relying on knowledge as the foundation of salvation, as the Gnostic heretics claim.

The Church is not merely theoretical knowledge about God, as the Gnostics imagined, which made them fall into false knowledge of Him, but she is a practical faith that appears in a life filled with righteousness and goodness, which we call the godly life, which is a great mystery that appeared in practice in the life of Christ on earth, and the verse shows it in the following stages:
(1) God was manifest in the flesh: the Second Hypostasis became incarnate, becoming in the likeness of men. This is a clear verse proving the divinity of Christ.
(2) Justified in the Spirit: the Holy Spirit bore witness to His righteousness.
(3) Seen of angels: the angels saw Him with us during His incarnation.

(4) Preached unto the Gentiles: the Messiah the Savior was proclaimed among the Gentiles and not among the Jews only. (5) Believed on in the world: all enjoy faith without favoring one nation over another. (6) Received up into glory: He ascended to heavenly glory.

Your steadfastness in the Church is steadfastness in the truth, so you live reassured and secure your eternity. So take care to attend the Church and to enjoy her Holy Sacraments, and submit to her teachings even if they conflict with some of your thoughts or personal aims.
Spiritual discipleship and rejecting the teachings of the heretics

entries.section: (1) Rejecting the words of the heretics

paragraphs.text: The Holy Spirit teaches the prophets about future matters, and so St. Paul taught clearly and prophesied that in the latter times, by which he means the times that extend from Christ’s ascension to His Second Coming, people will depart from the right faith delivered to the saints and follow the demons, who lead them astray from the way of Christ.

entries.section: (1) Rejecting the words of the heretics

paragraphs.text: Seared: burned with fire like skin, so that it loses its feeling; the meaning is that their consciences lose their feeling as if seared with a hot iron.
These deviant people will deceive the simple by acting out the godly life, while their consciences have lost all sense of responsibility, so they proclaim false teachings.

entries.section: (1) Rejecting the words of the heretics

paragraphs.text: The heretics (the Gnostics and the followers of Mani) proclaimed abstaining from marriage, considering marital relations unclean, and they held that it is not fitting for the perfect to partake of meats and some other foods. But Christians believe in the holiness of marriage and bodily relations, and that all foods are a gift from God, so they eat them with thanksgiving.

entries.section: (1) Rejecting the words of the heretics

paragraphs.text: We believe that God made everything good (Gen 1:31), and there is nothing unclean in His creation, and before we eat we pray and remember God’s blessing of the foods as it is written in the Holy Bible, then we eat and give thanks to God.

entries.section: (1) Rejecting the words of the heretics

paragraphs.text: The good shepherd is the one who speaks to the flock and reminds them of the right truths of the faith that they have already learned. By your commitment to this reminding of the believers, you will be a good minister of Jesus Christ, since you were brought up in the right faith and sound teachings, far from deceptions.

entries.section: (1) Rejecting the words of the heretics

paragraphs.text: Profane and old wives’ fables: pagan or Jewish ideas that the elderly pass on from their fathers, all of which are false and trivial matters that occupy a person and hinder him from his spiritual life, that is, they defile his mind with worthless thoughts.
Exercise thyself: strive by spiritual exercises to grow in virtue.

The Apostle warns Timothy not to be occupied with the ideas of pagans or Jews that are far from the truth, and to care for his goal, which is the spiritual life, and so to train himself to grow in it.

entries.section: (1) Rejecting the words of the heretics

paragraphs.text: That which is to come: eternal life.

Bodily exercise profits only the body, but godliness and the fear of God profit the whole being of man, that is, spirit and body together, for they purify his body, sanctify his thought, direct his will to the good and prepare him for eternal life.

Society may convey wrong ideas to you, so examine everything: does it agree with your faith and the teachings of the Church or not? And do not be distracted from your goal, which is the love of God, and so you advance at all times.

The faithful saying, worthy of all acceptation, is that godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come; it gives hope in the present life and leads to a happy eternal life.

The believer bears toil and insult for the sake of holding fast to the godly life, but his hope in Christ, who upholds him in afflictions, comforts his heart, because God upholds everyone who takes refuge in Him in affliction, and especially the believers.
He charges Timothy to teach the people all that has gone before in this chapter.

To the degree that you look to God, you can face afflictions and bear them, for He will uphold you and lighten them for you when you feel His presence with you, and in the end He will reward you with inexpressible blessings. So always remember that God is with you and does not leave you as long as you want Him.

Here St. Paul gives his disciple Timothy commandments that touch his spiritual striving, which are: Let no man despise thy youth: Timothy was young in age at the beginning of his episcopate, so the Apostle encourages him not to be concerned about this, since the power of Christ is with him and he carries out his pastoral ministry with confidence. An example in word: so that the words of God appear on his lips and his manner, being steady and precise. In conversation: his conduct is to be Christian according to God’s commandments.
In charity: his love for all appears, especially for those who wrong him.
In spirit: his spirituality appears in his worship and conduct.
In faith: in his teachings and in the face of difficult situations and afflictions.
In purity: the purity of his words and conduct from every evil aim.

He charges Timothy to care for reading the Holy Bible and meditating on it, the effect of which will appear in his preaching and teaching of the people, and to persevere in this until he meets Paul, who will complete his teaching and guidance.
The gift: the grace of the sacrament of the priesthood with all the gifts it carries, such as preaching and teaching.

Prophecy: there was a prophecy about Timothy that he would become a bishop and shepherd of God’s people. The laying on of the hands of the presbytery: when he was ordained bishop, Paul and the bishops with him laid their hands on him. This shows that ordination to the priesthood is by the laying on of the bishops’ hands on those presented for this rank. He calls him to use the gifts of God given to him in the priesthood, which God confirmed beforehand by prophecy, so that he may enjoy the work of God and benefit all those he shepherds.

He charges him to care for his ministry and to be wholly in it, that is, not to be occupied with any other works because he is consecrated to God, and by this he advances in his spiritual life and his ministry.

He also charges him with spiritual discipleship and constant learning from the Holy Bible and the teachings of the Apostle to him and benefiting from all people, and to the degree of his care for learning he will gain the salvation of his own soul and the salvation of the souls of those he shepherds.

If the bishop needs to continue in discipleship, reading and learning all the days of his life, then all the more do you need this, whatever your age or experience, because by this humility and your seeking the knowledge of God, He works in you by His Holy Spirit and guides you, so you delight in fellowship with Him, and those around you learn from your spirituality and come to God. So care not only for reading but also for observing the virtues of others, even children, so that you learn from every person.
Commandments for the elders, the widows and the priests

entries.section: (1) Treatment of the elderly and the young

paragraphs.text: The Apostle warns the shepherd Timothy to be wise in his dealing with every category of the flock, for shepherds are fathers responsible for all the people.
Rebuke not an elder: respecting the elderly and not reproving them harshly, but exhorting them as fathers who deserve honor for their age.
The younger men as brethren: the bishop’s humility appears not only with the elders but also with the young, so he treats them and teaches them as his brothers.
The elder women as mothers: treating and teaching elderly women as his mothers, with sufficient esteem and respect.
The younger as sisters: treating young women also with humility as his sisters, taking care over purity of heart, speech and conduct.

In your dealing with others, take care to honor the elderly and everyone who holds a position or has experience, for by this humility of yours you win everyone and learn from them, and you can draw them to Christ, and they esteem your words.
Honour: care for their needs.
Widows indeed: those who have no one to support them.
The Apostle directs Timothy’s attention to caring for widows who are in material need, providing for their needs.

The Apostle requires the believer whose mother or grandmother has been widowed to be committed to supporting her, for she is the one who served him and raised him in his childhood and youth. If she has become unable to provide for her needs because of her old age and the absence of anyone to support her, he must care for her in return for the toil she endured in raising him, for if he does so he does what is good and acceptable before God.

The Apostle stipulated that the one whom the Church helps must have no children or grandchildren able to support her, and that she has set her hope on the one who is truly able to support, and believes that God will not leave her alone, and continues in supplications and prayers without ceasing.
The widow absorbed in material things and in needless luxury is distracted from God by such conduct, so she dies spiritually.
Timothy, as a shepherd, is required to charge the widows to be in constant vigilance and to keep away from sin.

The believer is committed not only toward his mother or grandmother who is a widow, but toward the wider circle of those around him of relatives, especially his family, that is, those of his own house. For true faith moves a person toward love of others and care for them, especially those of his own house. And whoever does not behave so has denied the faith in practice in his life, and in this way becomes worse than an unbeliever, because even the pagan performs such duties toward his family and needy relatives.
The Apostle specified the conditions necessary for choosing the widow deaconess, which are:
Not under threescore years old: so that no one stumbles at her moving among the homes of those served and accompanying the priests when they visit some homes.

The wife of one man: she must not have been married more than once, as a proof of chastity and purity. This is the same condition that was followed with the bishop anciently and with the priest or full deacon to this day. Well reported of for good works: she has a witness from others to her practice of the virtues and her attachment to good works that show a heart wide in love for others.
And these works are:
If she have brought up children: her motherhood appeared in raising her children, or any children if she has no children in the flesh, with evident care and attention.
If she have lodged strangers: she cared for those who have no one with whom to stay, and welcomed any person who was a stranger to the Church in order to encourage him and provide for his needs.

If she have washed the saints’ feet: washing the feet of the believers as was the custom anciently when they entered homes, where their feet were soiled with dust from walking in open sandals. And not only this, but offering all services with humility however lowly these services may seem, such as cleaning the church and helping every needy person, sick person and bedridden person.
If she have relieved the afflicted: whether in troubles or in prisons, by meeting their needs and encouraging them.
If she have diligently followed every good work: she cared for works of goodness.
They have begun to wax wanton against Christ: they were distracted from Christ by the world and material things.

Young widows should not be consecrated for service, for the Apostle fears that after consecrating their lives to Christ they will turn back and want to marry, and so their covenant will be broken, and thus they become sinners and condemned before God for going back on their first covenant after pledging themselves to consecration to the service of the Lord.

Because these widows are not occupied with Christ and His service, their time becomes empty, so they go about from house to house, multiplying words and searching for the news of people and spending long time in frivolity.

I will therefore that the younger women marry, instead of idleness and not being occupied with service, so that they bear children and care for their little ones. Marriage is not forbidden, but is a fortress for them, so that no room is left for Satan to blaspheme God because of them. For God is not dishonored by the marriage of widows, but by their idleness and inner emptiness. And she who cannot occupy her time with raising her children and serving the Church is liable to turn away from Christ by falling into many sins, so in this case marriage is better for chastity than widowhood.
This does not mean that young widows must marry, because chastity and being occupied with Christ are better.

Here St. Paul returns to affirm the commitment of families to their widows: the Church is committed to give to the needy women who have no one to support them, while leaving the affairs of the needy women who do have someone to support them in the hands of their relatives who are able.

May you care for the needy among your relatives, not only materially but rather spiritually, so that you care for the salvation of those around you and invite them to attend the Church and enjoy the Holy Sacraments, and pray for them always.

entries.section: (3) Supporting the priests, trying them and ordaining them, with a special charge to Timothy

paragraphs.text: The elders: the correct translation here is “the priests.”

The Church is committed to meeting the material needs of the fathers the priests, so that they may devote themselves to preaching and teaching and not be burdened by the necessities of life. If the priests manage the spiritual affairs of the believers for their salvation, they must not be deprived of receiving their share of material needs, not that they may live in luxury but that they may have a decent living.

entries.section: (3) Supporting the priests, trying them and ordaining them, with a special charge to Timothy

paragraphs.text: This commandment came in the book of Deuteronomy (Deut 25:4); it is a figurative picture saying that when the ox draws the threshing implement, it should not be muzzled, so that it may fill its belly from the fruit of its labor. So also the minister: it is his right that his bodily needs be met by those he serves. And the Apostle quotes in this regard the saying of the Lord Christ in (Lk 10:7) that “the labourer is worthy of his hire.”

entries.section: (3) Supporting the priests, trying them and ordaining them, with a special charge to Timothy

paragraphs.text: An elder: what is meant by it here is the priest of the Church.

The Mosaic law required that no person be condemned without the testimony of two or three witnesses. Therefore the bishop should not be hasty in judging any priest, and should examine the complaint well.

entries.section: (3) Supporting the priests, trying them and ordaining them, with a special charge to Timothy

paragraphs.text: The Apostle asks his disciple Timothy, concerning those against whom the accusations are proved and were serious for the faith of the people, to rebuke them before the whole Church in order to preserve the soundness of the Church’s faith.

entries.section: (3) Supporting the priests, trying them and ordaining them, with a special charge to Timothy

paragraphs.text: In view of the priest’s standing and his influence on the people, St. Paul charges him before the Father and the Son and the holy angels not to give a judgment tainted by partiality or by bias to one side at the expense of the other, or with the aim of fulfilling personal desires.

entries.section: (3) Supporting the priests, trying them and ordaining them, with a special charge to Timothy

paragraphs.text: He advises him not to ordain a priest hastily, but to examine him well, because he is responsible for the ordination of everyone he ordains. If there are faults in him that make others stumble, he shares in his faults by ordaining him, so he warns him to keep himself pure by not taking part in ordaining others who are unsuitable for the ranks of the priesthood.

Beware of haste in your judgment of others, especially if they hold a position or great responsibility. If the matter does not concern you, do not interfere in it, and if it is necessary for you to take a position and a decision, examine the matter well, and prayer will support you and guide you to good thought and conduct.

entries.section: (3) Supporting the priests, trying them and ordaining them, with a special charge to Timothy

paragraphs.text: In consideration of Timothy’s illness, and out of St. Paul’s tenderness toward his sick disciple, he allowed him to drink a little wine as a remedy and not for pleasure. Here Paul’s fatherhood and his care for his son appear, not only in spiritual matters but also in bodily ones.

entries.section: (3) Supporting the priests, trying them and ordaining them, with a special charge to Timothy

paragraphs.text: Open beforehand: known to the general public.
Going before to judgment: deserving the Church’s judgment upon them.
And some men they follow after: their sins are not apparent and are hidden in their hearts, but God judges them, and they too are not fit for the priesthood.

In choosing priests, Paul charges Timothy not to ordain those who have sins apparent to people and deserving ecclesiastical punishment, and likewise those whose sins do not appear but are hidden in their hearts, by examining them carefully, because good works are plain before people, and so are evil works; whoever has good works he chooses for the priesthood, but whoever has evil works he rejects.
Christian conduct
Yoke: a piece of wood placed on the necks of the two animals that draw farm implements, and it signifies slavery, that is, that slaves are under the authority of their masters.

Without attacking the institution of slavery, the Apostle dealt with its problem by lifting the morale of the slaves and giving them guidance for a godly life that raises their souls above every material or psychological yoke, so that they live in obedience to their masters, lest the masters be given an opportunity to curse the new religion and the God whom they worship.

In the previous verse the Apostle spoke of the relation of slaves to their unbelieving masters, and here he speaks of the relation of slaves to their believing masters. He urges the slaves to give them full honor, because brotherhood in the faith does not mean that we deprive of honor those to whom honor is due; rather, we as slaves should serve them with greater diligence and faithfulness, because those who share in the blessings of salvation and in the communion of the Holy Sacraments are beloved believers who deserve all love and esteem from us. And Timothy is to teach and exhort these things so that doctrine may be translated into practical life and conduct.

Take care to honor those in authority, whether Christians or non-Christians, even if they are domineering and biased; by your love and longsuffering you will win everyone. Be faithful in your work and sincere in your relationships for God’s sake, whatever the mistakes of others, and so you present a living picture of the true Christian and glorify God’s name.
Proud: arrogant.
Strifes of words: continuing in quarrels.

St. Paul attacks the false teachers who leave the commandments of Christ and the teachings of righteousness and proclaim doctrines strange to the Church. These have fallen into pride and ignorance, and also into disputing and quarreling that breed many sins such as strife, envy and evil surmisings, and even reach to lying and slandering others, that is, they depart from love and divide the Church. And these, with their misleading, corrupt discussions, use godliness as a cover for trading in people and gaining positions and money, and they stray from true godliness. For this reason Paul warns Timothy against being troubled or having dealings with them.

Godliness from the Christian viewpoint is life with God, and it requires contentment in material things, that is, being satisfied with the material things God has bestowed on us. This is sound trade: seeking the salvation of the soul and keeping away from the love of money.

When a person is born, he has no money with him. And when he dies he takes nothing material with him, as Job said (Job 1:21). All this calls us not to cling to the love of money but to godliness and care for the spiritual life. If a person has his necessary needs of food and clothing, this suffices him to be occupied with his goal, that is, the salvation of his soul.
Destruction: corruption.

On the other hand, he warns the believers against the love of money and the desire for riches, for this exposes them to many temptations that lead them to perdition; for in their pursuit of riches they use wrong ways and are exposed to pride and various sins. More than this, the Apostle counts it among the mother sins that breed many evils, so that a person gives up his faith because the love of money has become his goal, and thereby his soul is tormented by the multitude of sins.

The whole world is under your feet, and you use it as you wish. But beware lest it master you and money become your goal, even under the name of raising the standard of living or acquiring modern devices, for by this you are distracted from your goal, who is God, and you gradually give up His commandments.

entries.section: (3) The striving of the children of God

paragraphs.text: The spiritual person flees from the love of money and pursues holiness and righteousness, and takes care to acquire the basic Christian virtues, which are faith in the mercies of the Lord, and love, which is the main foundation of true Christian life. He practices patience in bearing trials and sufferings, and is marked by meekness of heart and of feelings in his behavior toward others.

entries.section: (3) The striving of the children of God

paragraphs.text: Paul calls his disciple Timothy to hold fast to the Christian faith which he declared before the Church through his ministry and teachings, and to complete his spiritual striving for the salvation of his soul.

entries.section: (3) The striving of the children of God

paragraphs.text: A good confession: here the Apostle refers to Christ’s answer to Pilate when he asked Him, “Art thou a king then?” (Jn 18:37). He said, “To this end was I born,” and, “for this cause came I into the world, that I should bear witness unto the truth.” Likewise when they asked Him, “Art thou then the Son of God?” He answered, “Ye say that I am” (Lk 22:70). As Paul gives his disciple a weighty charge, he calls to witness God the Father, who gives life and gives resurrection from the dead, and His only-begotten Son Jesus Christ, who offered Himself as an example for us in bearing witness to the truth before Pontius Pilate. And the charge he gives him is that he carry out God’s commandments and live without spot or fault that could be a cause of blame directed at him by the flock or by God on the day of judgment. And he charges him to do this until the end of his life in the world, or until the Second Coming takes place, if that happens in his lifetime.

entries.section: (3) The striving of the children of God

paragraphs.text: The Second Coming of Christ will be shown by God in His appointed time, which He Himself fixed and which is known to Him alone, the blessed and only Potentate, the King of kings and Lord of lords. It is to be noted that the titles mentioned here are the very titles of God the Son as they occur in (Rev 17:14, 19:16), which show His glory and His authority over all creation.

entries.section: (3) The striving of the children of God

paragraphs.text: Christ has immortality, which He does not derive from anyone, and death cannot overcome Him; He dwells in the light which no man can approach unto, which even the angels cannot approach; no one has seen Him in His essence, nor can anyone see Him. We offer Him honor and the confession of His eternal power.

Care for your goal, which is eternity, where you will enjoy the vision of God and His inexpressible fellowship. Do not be lax in your striving to live righteousness, holiness and continual repentance, because the greatness of the Kingdom deserves that you labor today, for no labor can be measured against the glories of heaven.
This present world: life in the world.
Uncertain riches: that they not trust or rely on their wealth.

The Apostle charged the rich in the treasures that the world gives not to be puffed up in themselves, and not to let their possession of money drive them to excessive self-importance, and not to rely on their wealth, which they may lose in a single hour, affirming the necessity of setting all hope on God and not on money, God in whose hands is abundant good and who pours out upon us of His grace that we may enjoy His gifts.
It befits the rich to practice works of love whose credit remains forever, and to multiply good works, so that their hands give generously to the needy.
The giving of the rich lays up for them a treasure in heaven which they will enjoy, and a foundation on which they rely for entering the Kingdom.
If God has given you money or abilities, you are a steward over them, to use them in helping those around you, for by works of mercy you can enter heaven. So seize every opportunity to do good.

That which is committed to thy trust: the oral teachings that Paul taught to Timothy, which are called the tradition of the Church. The Apostle ends his epistle to his disciple, asking him to keep the living faith that was delivered to the saints and to avoid the foolish discussions of the false teachers, who exchanged faith for knowledge and so fell into falsely so called knowledge.

As some of them, like the Gnostics, claimed to have attained knowledge, they wandered in the mazes of this satanic, misleading knowledge; and while they were seeking salvation through knowledge, they failed utterly and lost the doctrine of sound faith and the knowledge of God.
The Apostle ends his epistle with the apostolic blessing and his asking grace for his disciple.

Hold fast to the teachings you hear in the Church so that you live them, and take care to know God so that you love Him, and keep away from the debates of learning that do not lead you to God, even if they are spiritual sciences.
